question: On 13 January 2024, the people of Taiwan elected Lai Ching-te, a member of the Democratic Progressive Party, as their new president. Lai Ching-te does not support the policy of reunification with the People’s Republic of China. In response, Beijing reiterated its objective of fully reintegrating the island democracy into the People’s Republic of China.

Taiwan has gained considerable importance in recent years thanks to the manufacture of microprocessors and strategic components for both civilian and military industries. The island enjoys a virtual monopoly in this field, supplying 50 % of global demand.
What measures does the Commission intend to take, if it has not already done so, to ensure the supply of micro-processors to European companies, despite these tensions?
answer: The Commission is aware of the strategic role of Taiwan in the production of semiconductors. In this context, it has undertaken a number of initiatives aimed at building and reinforcing semiconductor supply chains and cooperation with Taiwan.

As part of the trade and investment dialogue with Taiwan, the Commission set up in 2022 a dedicated dialogue on semiconductors, which has been followed up through discussions in the Government/Authorities Meeting on Semiconductors (GAMS) and direct engagement with industry.

Semiconductors and the EU Chips Act (1) were also one of the focus areas of the European Innovation Week, organised in May/June 2023, as well as the 4th European Investment Forum on 12 October 2023, both held in Taipei. Both events attracted very high interest and were attended by top officials and industry representatives.

In line with the Global Approach to Research and Innovation (2) and the EU strategy for cooperation in the Indo-Pacific (3), the Commission has launched a series of research and innovation initiatives to increase the participation of Taiwan in Horizon Europe and to support technical cooperation among researchers and entities based in the EU and Taiwan.

Research and innovation collaboration is also supported by the exchange programme Erasmus for Young Entrepreneurs Global (4). This exchange programme gives experienced entrepreneurs based in Taiwan the opportunity to collaborate with new entrepreneurs from the EU.

Thanks to EU efforts such as the EU Chips Act, Taiwan semiconductor manufacturing company has decided to invest in a semiconductor factory in Dresden, Germany. Taiwanese chemicals suppliers to the semiconductor industry have also announced an interest to invest in the EU.
